paragraphs: Online learning involves choosing actions repeatedly while learning from their losses. Some sequences are easier to learn from than others: losses may follow a stable stochastic process, or the differences between available actions may remain small. This paper asks how a learner with limited observations can benefit from both kinds of favorable structure.

The authors introduce Second Order Difference Adjustments, or SODA. Its key resource is one additional observation per round beyond standard bandit feedback. They prove that this extra observation is sufficient to overcome an impossibility result that prevents ordinary bandit algorithms from obtaining regret proportional to the effective loss range. SODA does not need that range supplied beforehand.

The resulting guarantees combine protection against an unrestricted oblivious adversary with improved bounds for stochastic losses and adversarial losses with small effective range. A lower bound almost matches the adversarial upper bound. Together, these results show that a modest increase in feedback can enable adaptation to easier data without requiring the learner to choose between the two guarantees.
neurips-2018-adaptation-to-easy-data-in-.tldr: SODA uses one extra observation per round to improve regret on two kinds of easy data while retaining an adversarial guarantee.

paragraphs: Residual networks train layers to make corrections to earlier outputs. This suggests that adding residual layers should preserve the performance available from a simpler network. However, the training problem is nonconvex, so the ability to represent a good solution does not by itself establish that training avoids poor local minima.

The paper proves a result about this optimization landscape: for the residual networks studied, no local minimum has an objective value worse than what a linear predictor can attain. The result covers arbitrarily deep, nonlinear residual units under minimal or no assumptions on the particular architecture, data distribution, or loss function. The authors also quantify the behavior of approximate stationary points.

A separate result addresses training directly. With a particular architectural modification, standard stochastic gradient descent reaches an objective value close to or better than any linear predictor. This distinction matters: a statement about local minima and a statement about an optimization algorithm are different guarantees. Neither claim requires residual networks to strictly outperform linear prediction in every problem.
neurips-2018-are-resnets-provably-better.tldr: The paper establishes a linear-predictor benchmark for residual-network local minima and, with an architectural modification, for stochastic gradient descent.

paragraphs: Distributed stochastic gradient descent lets multiple clients contribute to learning a shared model. When those clients are mobile devices, the information they transmit must serve two goals: use little communication and protect client privacy. The paper addresses these requirements together, whereas the prior methods described in the abstract had established one property without establishing the other.

The authors study algorithms that combine communication efficiency with differential privacy. For a problem with d variables and approximately d clients, their proposed method requires O(log log(nd)) transmitted bits per client per coordinate while maintaining constant privacy. This is a conditional communication guarantee tied to the stated relationship between client count and problem dimension.

The paper also sharpens the analysis of the Binomial mechanism. It shows nearly the utility of the Gaussian mechanism while using fewer bits to represent the privatized values. That result matters because privacy mechanisms must ultimately produce information that devices can transmit: the numerical representation is part of the communication cost, alongside the learning algorithm itself.
neurips-2018-cpsgd-communication-efficie.tldr: cpSGD combines differential privacy with low communication costs and strengthens the utility analysis of the compact Binomial mechanism.

paragraphs: A textual network contains both connections between vertices and text associated with them. Learning a compact vector for each vertex therefore involves deciding how these two information sources should interact. The paper argues that methods focused on text relationships along individual edges miss the broader connectivity that can help establish semantic relatedness.

Diffusion Maps for Textual Network Embedding, or DMTE, incorporates global graph structure into the treatment of text. A diffusion-convolution operation acts on the text inputs, allowing their representations to reflect connectivity beyond a single edge. The method also introduces an objective that uses graph diffusion to preserve higher-order proximity efficiently.

This approach matters because two texts can be related through the surrounding network even when a direct connection provides an incomplete picture. The reported experiments show improvements over the compared state-of-the-art methods on vertex classification and link prediction. Those findings support the usefulness of combining textual information with broader graph relationships for the evaluated tasks, rather than treating local text pairs as the whole source of structure.
neurips-2018-diffusion-maps-for-textual-.tldr: DMTE uses graph diffusion to combine text with global network structure, improving reported vertex-classification and link-prediction results.

paragraphs: Keypoints provide a compact way to describe an object's geometry, but choosing which points to detect can itself be a learning problem. KeypointNet learns both a category-specific set of points and detectors that predict their three-dimensional positions from one two-dimensional image. The aim is to discover points useful for geometric reasoning.

The framework is trained through a differentiable pose objective that evaluates how well the keypoints recover the relative pose between two views of an object. This connects the choice of points directly to the task they should support. The network discovers consistent points across different views of one object and across different instances within an object category.

The authors report that this end-to-end approach, without ground-truth keypoint annotations, outperforms a fully supervised baseline using the same network architecture on pose estimation. This comparison suggests that points selected through the geometric task can be more useful than the annotated points used by that baseline. The paper presents discovered keypoints for cars, chairs, and planes from ShapeNet.
neurips-2018-discovery-of-latent-3d-keyp.tldr: KeypointNet discovers consistent 3D keypoints through a pose objective and outperforms a supervised pose-estimation baseline without keypoint annotations.

paragraphs: Word embeddings describe words as vectors, while topic models describe topics through distributions over words. This paper joins the two by using distances between word vectors as the underlying distances in a Wasserstein topic model. The geometry of the embeddings thereby becomes part of how topic and document distributions are compared.

The framework jointly learns word embeddings, topic distributions, and optimal transports connecting topics to documents. Its distillation mechanism supplies a ground-distance matrix for updating topics and smoothly computing the associated transports. These calculations then guide the embedding updates. The authors describe this guidance as more robust and report that it improves algorithm convergence.

The application uses patient admission records, treating disease and procedure codes as the elements to embed and learning topics of admissions. The paper reports superior performance on constructing clinically meaningful disease networks, predicting mortality from admission codes, and recommending procedures. These findings support the joint learning approach in the evaluated setting: the learned relationships between codes and the learned admission topics inform one another.
neurips-2018-distilled-wasserstein-learn.tldr: A distilled Wasserstein framework jointly learns embeddings and topics, with reported improvements on several tasks using patient admission records.

paragraphs: Bandit learning involves choosing actions while receiving only limited feedback about their rewards. This paper considers actions built by combining smaller, atomic choices. Its factored-bandit model represents the action space as a Cartesian product, giving the learning problem an explicit structure even when the set of complete actions contains many combinations.

The model includes rank-one bandits as a special case while substantially relaxing their assumptions about the reward function. For stochastic factored bandits, the authors provide an anytime algorithm, which can operate without a predetermined stopping horizon. They establish upper and lower regret bounds that match up to constant factors, characterizing the achievable learning performance within this problem formulation.

A small modification also makes the algorithm applicable to utility-based dueling bandits. In that setting, the authors improve additive terms in the regret bound relative to existing algorithms. These terms can dominate until horizons exponential in the number of arms, so improving them can matter across a substantial range of learning durations, rather than only changing a negligible part of the guarantee.
neurips-2018-factored-bandits-71e05af755.tldr: Factored bandits model actions assembled from atomic choices and admit an anytime algorithm with regret bounds matching up to constants.

paragraphs: A recommendation strategy can change the preferences it is trying to satisfy. Repeated exposure may make a user bored, while a strategy can become appealing again after a break. This paper questions the assumption that a recommender should identify one best fixed strategy and then continue using it indefinitely.

The authors model recommendation as a Markov decision process whose rewards depend linearly on recent actions. This makes the history of recommendations relevant to both present and future outcomes. They show that a policy accounting for these longer-term effects may outperform a fixed-action policy and a contextual greedy policy. Alternating strategies can therefore be useful when the modeled preference dynamics apply.

To learn in an unknown environment, the paper introduces LINUCRL, an extension of UCRL that balances exploration with exploitation. Its regret bound does not depend on the number of states. Empirical evaluations in realistic scenarios support the model assumptions and algorithm. The contribution links boredom-sensitive recommendation to a learnable sequential decision problem with both theoretical and empirical support.
neurips-2018-fighting-boredom-in-recomme.tldr: A history-dependent recommendation model and LINUCRL algorithm account for boredom and the long-term effects of alternating strategies.

paragraphs: In nonconvex optimization, a small gradient does not necessarily indicate a useful stopping point: a saddle point can also have little first-order signal. This theory paper develops stochastic algorithms that use first-order information to escape non-degenerate saddle points and obtain a stronger, second-order form of stationarity.

The central construction, NEON, starts from noise and follows a principled sequence of first-order operations to extract negative curvature associated with the Hessian. Negative curvature identifies a direction relevant to leaving a saddle. The authors use this construction in a general framework that upgrades existing algorithms whose guarantees may stop at first-order stationary points.

With high probability, the resulting methods can find a point whose gradient norm is at most epsilon and whose Hessian has no eigenvalue below negative square root of epsilon. The best stated time complexity is Õ(d/epsilon^3.5), nearly linear in dimension d. The authors describe this as the first such dimensional dependence for first-order stochastic methods, and as competitive with stochastic methods that use second-order information.
neurips-2018-first-order-stochastic-algo.tldr: NEON extracts negative-curvature information through first-order operations, enabling stochastic saddle escape with nearly linear dependence on dimension.

paragraphs: Neural conversation models can produce responses that offer little information or vary too little across conversations. The paper treats informativeness and diversity as related but distinct goals. A method aimed at improving one therefore needs an explicit account of how it addresses the other, rather than relying on a single undifferentiated notion of response quality.

Adversarial Information Maximization, or AIM, combines two training components. Adversarial training encourages the distribution of generated responses to match the distribution of real responses, addressing diversity. A separate objective increases a variational lower bound on mutual information between a query and its response. This connects informativeness to how much information the paired utterances share.

The contribution is the combination of these objectives in one adversarial learning framework. It addresses variation among generated responses while also encouraging responses to carry information about their particular queries. Automatic evaluations and human assessments both show significant improvements in informativeness and diversity. These are empirical findings for the evaluated methods, supporting the proposed separation and joint treatment of the two goals.
neurips-2018-generating-informative-and-.tldr: AIM combines adversarial response matching with a mutual-information objective to improve conversational diversity and informativeness in evaluations.

paragraphs: Gaussian process inference can be expensive even when the model itself has been designed to scale. This paper focuses on the computational machinery used for training and prediction, asking how it can better exploit modern hardware. Its proposed approach, Blackbox Matrix-Matrix multiplication, or BBMM, organizes inference around matrix-matrix operations.

BBMM uses a modified, batched conjugate-gradients algorithm to obtain all terms needed for training and inference in a single call. The paper states that this reduces the asymptotic cost of exact Gaussian process inference from cubic to quadratic in the number of observations. A specialized preconditioner further accelerates convergence of the iterative computation.

The same approach can support scalable approximations and complex Gaussian process models when efficient multiplication routines are available for their kernel matrices and derivatives. Experiments demonstrate substantial GPU acceleration for both exact inference and approximations. The authors also introduce GPyTorch, a PyTorch-based platform implementing this approach. The contribution thus joins a computational framework, a reusable interface for different models, and an accompanying software platform.
neurips-2018-gpytorch-blackbox-matrix-ma.tldr: BBMM reorganizes Gaussian process inference around GPU-friendly matrix operations, with quadratic stated complexity and implementation in GPyTorch.

paragraphs: An initial value problem specifies how a system changes and where its trajectory begins. Numerical integration approximates that trajectory through successive time steps. This paper develops probabilistic integrators for such problems, using the multistep Adams–Moulton method as the starting point for a new family of implicit constructions.

The defining feature is that a step can incorporate feedback from the forthcoming time point. The abstract contrasts this with earlier probabilistic integrators, which used explicit methods. The authors adapt previous probabilistic-solver work to this implicit setting and rigorously establish that their construction is well defined and convergent. This provides mathematical support for the method alongside its algorithmic description.

The paper also discusses calibration: how the probabilistic treatment should be set, rather than merely introducing randomness into a solver. It suggests one approach and illustrates the effects of probabilistic integration in an inverse problem involving parameter inference. That example connects the solver to a downstream task, showing why the treatment of numerical integration can matter when estimating the parameters of a dynamical system.
neurips-2018-implicit-probabilistic-inte.tldr: The paper introduces implicit probabilistic ODE integrators, proves their convergence, and illustrates their role in parameter inference.

paragraphs: Importance sampling had been used to improve variational bounds on likelihoods, but that leaves a separate question: how should these ideas be understood when the goal is probabilistic inference itself? This paper clarifies that connection through Importance Weighted Variational Inference, or IWVI, linking the weighting technique to a broader variational formulation.

The central theoretical observation is that IWVI is an instance of augmented variational inference. Viewing it this way identifies looseness in earlier work and makes the relationship between the inference procedure and its variational interpretation more explicit. Experiments then support IWVI as a practical method for probabilistic inference, complementing the conceptual analysis with evidence of usability.

A second contribution examines inference using elliptical distributions. The authors report improved accuracy in low-dimensional settings and improved convergence in high-dimensional settings. These are distinct benefits associated with different dimensional regimes. Together, the contributions address both the formulation of importance-weighted inference and the choice of distributions used for inference, showing that each can affect the resulting procedure.
neurips-2018-importance-weighting-and-va.tldr: The paper interprets IWVI as augmented variational inference and reports dimension-dependent benefits from using elliptical distributions.

paragraphs: Weather radar archives contain detailed measurements relevant to bird migration, but their velocity observations are partial. Historically, modeling and computational constraints led researchers to summarize velocities at only a few locations, discarding much of the available spatial detail. This paper develops a model intended to reconstruct full velocity fields at high resolution across the United States.

The proposed Gaussian process treats the sources of complexity jointly. It accounts for spatially random velocities, partial observations, the geometry of individual radar stations, measurement noise, and aliasing ambiguity. Bringing these elements into one framework connects the desired full velocity field to the particular measurements that the radar network actually supplies.

Efficient computation is another central contribution. The authors develop inference algorithms based on the fast Fourier transform, using Laplace's method to work around the non-stationary kernel of the joint process. The resulting approach addresses both representation and computation: it models the observation process while providing a route to inference at the spatial scale that earlier summaries could not retain.
neurips-2018-inferring-latent-velocities.tldr: A joint Gaussian process model and FFT-based inference reconstruct full velocity fields from partial, noisy weather-radar observations.

paragraphs: A convex polytope can be described by intersecting halfspaces, with each halfspace imposing a linear boundary. This paper studies how to learn such a shape from labeled data when the data have a margin. It works in the realizable PAC setting, where a suitable target polytope can account for the labels.

The proposed algorithm properly learns the class: its output is itself a polytope. If an optimal polytope uses t halfspaces, the algorithm constructs a consistent polytope using about t log t halfspaces with margins, in time polynomial in t. Thus, the guarantee permits a more complex output boundary than the optimal polytope while retaining consistency with the supplied data.

The paper also examines what a margin should mean for a polytope. A definition familiar from a single hyperplane does not yield only one possible extension to an intersection of halfspaces. The authors identify distinct generalizations and study their geometric relationships. This analysis helps specify the learning assumptions precisely and may also be useful for geometric questions beyond learning.
neurips-2018-learning-convex-polytopes-w.tldr: Under realizability and margin assumptions, the algorithm learns a consistent polytope with about t log t halfspaces in time polynomial in t.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a complete three-dimensional object from one image requires reasoning about surfaces the image does not show. Learned shape priors can supply that information, but they may become strongly tied to the object categories used during training. This paper introduces Generalizable Reconstruction, or GenRe, to learn priors that are less category-specific.

GenRe combines several representations within its inference network and training procedure. Depth and silhouette describe visible surfaces in a 2.5D form. Spherical representations cover visible and hidden surfaces, while voxels represent three-dimensional shape. The combination is organized around the causal relationship between a three-dimensional object and the two-dimensional image it produces, giving the representations complementary roles.

The experiments show that GenRe performs well at single-view reconstruction and generalizes to diverse objects from categories absent during training. This supports the intended benefit of learning more generic shape knowledge: reconstruction can remain useful beyond the categories that supplied the training examples. The finding concerns demonstrated generalization to novel objects, without asserting that every unseen category will be reconstructed equally well.
neurips-2018-learning-to-reconstruct-sha.tldr: GenRe combines complementary geometric representations to reconstruct 3D shapes from single images and generalize to unseen object categories.

paragraphs: Understanding a complex image involves identifying objects and interpreting their relationships. Because the objects influence how the whole scene is understood, predicting each label independently can miss relevant context. This paper uses structured prediction, which treats the output as an interconnected collection of labels and explicitly models interactions within that collection.

The authors propose permutation invariance as a principle for designing deep structured-prediction architectures. The ordering used to represent a scene's elements should not change the underlying interpretation. They prove a necessary and sufficient characterization of architectures satisfying the relevant invariance requirement, then discuss how that result guides model design.

The resulting model achieves a new state of the art on the Visual Genome scene graph labeling benchmark, outperforming the recent approaches included in the comparison. The paper therefore connects an architectural principle to both a mathematical characterization and an evaluated model. Its significance is that a natural structural requirement can provide concrete guidance for combining deep learning components, rather than leaving their organization entirely to experimentation.
neurips-2018-mapping-images-to-scene-gra.tldr: A permutation-invariance characterization guides a scene-graph architecture that achieves state-of-the-art results on the reported Visual Genome benchmark.

paragraphs: Expert demonstrations can contain several distinct ways to act successfully. This paper proposes an imitation-learning framework that can represent such multimodal behavior while assigning probability to only a selected set of actions. Its organizing objective is maximum causal Tsallis entropy, abbreviated MCTE.

The authors prove that the optimal solution has a sparsemax distribution with an adjustable supporting set. Unlike softmax, this distribution can assign exactly zero probability to unnecessary actions. They also establish an equivalence between the MCTE problem and robust Bayes estimation under the Brier score, giving the framework a second mathematical interpretation beyond its entropy-based formulation.

The practical MCTEIL algorithm uses a sparse mixture density network whose mixture weights follow sparsemax. The paper shows that causal Tsallis entropy encourages exploration and efficient use of mixture components, with Boltzmann–Gibbs entropy being less effective in this role. In two simulation studies, MCTEIL outperforms existing imitation-learning methods on average returns and learning multimodal policies. These results connect the theoretical sparsity property to demonstrated policy-learning benefits.
neurips-2018-maximum-causal-tsallis-entr.tldr: MCTEIL uses Tsallis entropy and sparsemax mixture weights to learn sparse, multimodal policies, with improvements in two simulation studies.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning usually lacks a teacher that supplies the true value of a state or action. Algorithms instead learn from a return: an approximation combining sampled experience with estimated values. Choices about discounting future rewards and bootstrapping from current estimates therefore help determine what the algorithm learns and how it behaves.

This paper introduces a gradient-based meta-learning method that adapts the return while the agent interacts with its environment. Rather than treating the learning target's construction as fixed throughout training, the method makes it part of the adaptation process. The motivation is that decisions shaping the return are crucial to the success of reinforcement learning.

The authors evaluate the algorithm on 57 Atari 2600 games over 200 million frames and report a new state-of-the-art performance. The result supports online adaptation of the return as a useful component in the evaluated setting. The broader contribution is a way to learn aspects of the learning process itself, alongside the estimates or policies being improved through experience.
neurips-2018-meta-gradient-reinforcement.tldr: Meta-gradient reinforcement learning adapts the return online and achieves a reported state-of-the-art result across 57 Atari games.

paragraphs: Imitation learning aims to recover a policy from expert demonstrations without an available reward signal. Extending it to several interacting agents introduces additional difficulties. Multiple Nash equilibria can provide different patterns of behavior, and each agent faces an environment affected by the others, making the learning situation non-stationary.

The paper proposes a multi-agent imitation-learning framework for general Markov games. It builds on a generalized form of inverse reinforcement learning, extending the conceptual basis for learning from demonstrations to settings with interacting decision makers. The authors also introduce a practical multi-agent actor-critic algorithm to turn that framework into a learning procedure.

The method is presented as applicable to complex behaviors in high-dimensional environments involving cooperative or competing agents. The abstract reports good empirical performance for the practical algorithm. The contribution is therefore both a framework for formulating imitation across multiple agents and an algorithm with experimental support. Its scope includes different relationships among agents, rather than assuming that all participants necessarily share the same objective.
neurips-2018-multi-agent-generative-adve.tldr: The paper extends imitation learning to general Markov games and introduces an empirically effective actor-critic algorithm for interacting agents.

paragraphs: Maximum inner product search asks which stored vectors have the largest inner product with a query. It resembles nearest-neighbor search, but inner products do not form a proper metric. This difference complicates the use of methods designed around metric distances, even though fast retrieval is important in many machine-learning applications.

The paper extends similarity graphs to this non-metric setting. Such graphs connect each vertex to vertices judged most similar under a chosen function. The proposed method works directly with the original data, without transforming maximum inner product search into a nearest-neighbor problem. The authors also explain why that transformation is detrimental when using similarity graphs.

An extensive experimental comparison reports a major improvement in the trade-off between runtime and accuracy over existing approaches. The significance is not only faster search in the evaluated comparisons, but also the suitability of using the original similarity relationship when constructing the graph. The work demonstrates that a framework originally proposed for metric spaces can be extended effectively to this non-metric retrieval problem.
neurips-2018-non-metric-similarity-graph.tldr: Similarity graphs applied directly to original vectors substantially improve the reported runtime–accuracy trade-off for maximum inner product search.

paragraphs: A neural network's success on familiar data does not establish how it behaves on inputs from another distribution. This paper addresses detecting those unfamiliar examples by changing the representation of the labels used as training targets. The central idea is to provide several dense semantic descriptions of each label instead of a sparse representation.

These target descriptions come from word representations learned using different corpora or architectures. Using several representations gives the model multiple semantic versions of the same target label. The proposed approach therefore makes the label space itself part of the detection method, connecting predictions to meaning-bearing vectors rather than relying on only a sparse class identifier.

The authors evaluate the method on computer-vision and speech-command detection tasks. Their results suggest favorable performance compared with previous methods, a qualified empirical claim rather than a universal advantage. They also present its effectiveness for identifying incorrectly classified examples and adversarial examples. Together, the evaluations examine whether the changed targets help recognize several kinds of problematic inputs or predictions.
neurips-2018-out-of-distribution-detecti.tldr: Multiple semantic label representations show promise for detecting out-of-distribution, misclassified, and adversarial examples.

paragraphs: Data poisoning changes a model's eventual behavior by introducing selected examples into its training data. This paper studies targeted attacks that affect a particular test instance while preserving overall classifier performance. The injected examples retain correct labels, so the attacker does not need control over the process that assigns training labels.

The authors present an optimization-based method for constructing these clean-label examples. In the transfer-learning setting they demonstrate that a single poisoned image can control the classifier's behavior on the chosen target. For full end-to-end training, they introduce a watermarking strategy that makes poisoning reliable using approximately 50 training examples. The two findings concern different training settings and different amounts of poisoned data.

The demonstration uses poisoned frog images from CIFAR to manipulate image classifiers. The abstract also identifies a possible route into training sets: correctly labeled images placed online could later be collected by scraping. The results show why correct labels and preserved overall performance do not, by themselves, rule out targeted manipulation of a particular prediction.
neurips-2018-poison-frogs-targeted-clean.tldr: Correctly labeled poisoned images can manipulate a chosen test prediction, with distinct demonstrations for transfer learning and end-to-end training.

paragraphs: A backdoor attack can leave a neural network behaving normally on ordinary inputs while causing a different output when an attacker-supplied perturbation appears. This makes routine behavior on benign data an incomplete indicator of whether training data have been poisoned. The paper investigates a detectable property of the poisoning behind these attacks.

The authors identify what they call spectral signatures in all backdoor attacks known to them. These signatures provide a basis for using robust-statistical tools to detect and remove poisoned training examples. The contribution connects a property of the malicious data to a defensive procedure, rather than relying only on observing the network's behavior on typical inputs.

Experiments on real image datasets and state-of-the-art neural-network architectures demonstrate the effectiveness of this detection and removal approach. The authors view the finding as an initial step toward a principled account of backdoor attacks. The scope of the central observation is the known attacks examined by the work; it does not establish that every possible future backdoor must expose the same signature.
neurips-2018-spectral-signatures-in-back.tldr: Spectral signatures found in known backdoor attacks enable robust-statistical detection and removal of poisoned examples in image experiments.

paragraphs: Many prediction problems provide detailed inputs but only coarse outputs. Disease mapping, for example, may require fine-scale predictions even though observed outcomes are aggregated. This mismatch makes learning harder because the model must connect individual inputs to measurements that summarize groups of them, rather than observing a matching output for each input.

The paper combines Gaussian processes with an explicit model of output aggregation and variational learning. Aggregation makes standard evidence lower bounds intractable, so the authors derive new bounds and workable approximations. These changes support learning while explicitly accounting for uncertainty, and the framework accommodates several likelihood types, including a Poisson model for aggregated counts.

The authors report improved predictive accuracy and scalability to large datasets. They apply the framework to fine-scale spatial modeling of malaria incidence using more than one million observations. This application demonstrates the intended use: extracting finer-grained predictive information from coarser outcome measurements. The contribution addresses both the statistical mismatch between inputs and outputs and the computational difficulty introduced by modeling their aggregation.
neurips-2018-variational-learning-on-agg.tldr: New variational bounds enable scalable Gaussian process learning from aggregated outputs, including fine-scale malaria modeling with over one million observations.
